div.p: Priority-based 1 Functional Reactive Programming (P-FRP) is a new functional programming formalism for developing safety-critical embedded systems. P-FRP allows static priority assignment and guarantees real-time response by preempting lower priority tasks. Due to the state-less nature of functional programs, preempted tasks in P-FRP are aborted and have to restart after the higher priority tasks have completed execution. Since the execution semantics of P-FRP are different from the classical preemptive model of execution, existing utilization based sufficient conditions cannot be applied. In this paper, we derive a new utilization based sufficient schedulability condition for P-FRP, and validate it using experimental task sets.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Functional Reactive Programming (FRP) [15] is a declarative programming language for modeling and implementing safety-critical embedded systems. It has been used for a wide range of applications, notably, graphics [1], robotics [10], and vision [11]. FRP elegantly captures continuous and discrete aspects of a hybrid system using the notions of behavior and event, respectively. Because this language is developed as an embedded language in Haskell, it benefits from the wealth of abstractions provided in this language. Unfortunately, Haskell provides no real-time guarantees, and therefore neither does FRP.

To address this limitation, resource-bounded variants of FRP were studied ( [8], [13], [14]). Recently, it was shown that a variant called priority-based FRP (P-FRP) [8] combines both the semantic properties for FRP, guarantees resource boundedness, and supports assigning different priorities to different events. In P-FRP, higher priority events can preempt lower-priority ones. However, to maintain guarantees of type safety and state-less execution, the functional programming paradigm requires the execution of a function to continue uninterrupted. To comply with this requirement, as well as allow preemption of lower priority events, P-FRP implements a transactional model of execution. Using only a copy of the state during event execution and atomically committing these changes at the end of the event handler (or task), P-FRP ensures that handling an event is an "all or nothing" proposition. This preserves the easily understandable semantics of the FRP and provides a programming model where response times to different events can be tweaked by the programmer, without ever affecting the semantic soundness of the program.

In their seminal paper, Liu and Layland [9] derived the sufficient conditions for fixed priority rate-monotonic (RM) and dynamic priority Earliest-Deadline-First (EDF) scheduling under the preemptive execution model. The derivations presented by Liu and Layland were based on the notion of critical instant, which is the instance of release of higher priority tasks that leads to the worst-case response time (WCRT) of a lower priority task. For preemptive execution, Liu and Layland showed that the critical instance of release is when all tasks are released synchronously (at the same time). However due to the abort nature of preemption, a synchronous release does not lead to the WCRT in P-FRP (see Section 2.3 for example). Therefore, the utilization based sufficient condition derived for the preemptive model do not hold true in P-FRP, and new conditions are required.
Previous works on P-FRP ( [8], [12]) only provide basic scheduling conditions as well as algorithms for determining actual or bounded response times.

div.head: A. CONTRIBUTIONS
div.p: In this paper, we derive a utilization based scheduling condition for P-FRP task sets. This utilization based sufficient scheduling condition has not been derived before. After presenting the basic concepts and execution model of P-FRP (Section 2.1 and Section 2.2), we show that a synchronous release of higher priority tasks does not lead to the WCRT in P-FRP (Section 2.3). We highlight basic schedulability characteristic of P-FRP tasks (Section 3), through which we identify a worst-case release condition. The worstcase release condition is used for deriving schedulability condition of task sets with two tasks (Section 4). This is followed by deriving the schedulability condition when more than two tasks are present (Section 5). The results are validated using synthetic task sets of various sizes (Section 6). We conclude with a review of related work (Section 7) and a reflection on our results (Section 8).

div.head: II. BASIC CONCEPTS AND EXECUTION MODEL
div.p: In this section, we introduce the basic concepts and the notation used to denote these concepts in the rest of the paper. In addition, we review the P-FRP execution model.

div.head: B. EXECUTION MODEL AND ASSUMPTIONS
div.p: In this study, all tasks are assumed to execute in a uniprocessor system. When job of a higher priority task W i is released, it can immediately preempt an executing lower priority task, and changes made by the lower priority task are rolled back. The lower priority task will be restarted after the higher priority task has completed execution. All tasks are assumed to run without precedence constraints.

When some task is released, it enters an execution queue which is arranged by priority order such that all arriving higher priority tasks are moved to the head of the queue. The length of the queue is bounded and no two instances of the same task can be present in the queue at the same time. This requires a task to complete execution before the release of its next job. To maintain this requirement we assume a hard real-time system with task deadline equal to the time period between jobs. Hence, W k * n , D k = T k . All time parameters have discrete integer values.

Once W i enters the queue, two situations are possible. If a task of lower priority than i is being executed, it will be immediately preempted and W i will start. If a task of higher priority than W i is being executed, then W i will wait in the queue and start execution only after the higher priority task has completed. In P-FRP, when a task starts execution it creates a 'scratch' state, which is a copy of the current state of the system. Changes made during the execution of this task are maintained inside such a state, and the copy is done in an atomic operation. When the task has completed, the 'scratch' state is restored into the final state, also in an atomic operation.

Hence, a higher priority task may experience some blocking overhead if it is released when the lower priority task is in the copy or restore phase. These blocking overheads are a small fraction of the execution time of tasks and have not been considered in this paper. Sufficient conditions for P-FRP with consideration of these overheads will be derived as an future extensions to this work.

div.head: C. CRITICAL INSTANT IN P-FRP
div.p: In response time analysis for fixed-priority scheduling, a critical-instant of release is assumed. Critical instant is the time at which task releases lead to the WCRT of a lower priority task. Liu and Layland showed that in fixed-priority scheduling for the preemptive model, the critical-instant occurs when all tasks are released synchronously. In P-FRP, a synchronous release does not lead to the WCRT for all cases. Consider the following example:

div.head: VI. EXPERIMENTAL RESULTS
div.p: We present the experimental results using synthetic task sets in this section. The bounds were validated by making sure that all task sets which satisfy the sufficient conditions were schedulable in all release scenarios. The task periods and execution times were randomly selected from the ranges [20,70] and [3,15] respectively. These ranges were arbitrarily chosen and kept small to reduce the time taken in computing the results. The generated task sets were unique in the sense that at least one task is different between any two task sets.
For validating the sufficient bound, 1000 task sets were generated, each for 2-task, 3-task and 4-task sets. The task periods in each task set * n were selected such that:
div.formula: n•T 1 t T i W i * n .
div.p: All task sets had total utilization factor U less than or equal to the sufficient bound. Hence, the U of tasks sets were less than or equal to 0.5, 0.33 and 0.25 for 2-task, 3task and 4-task sets respectively. The WCRT values of the P-FRP task sets were computed by analyzing all release scenarios. In fig. 4, we show the difference between the deadline and the WCRT of W 1 (∆). A positive value of ∆ implies a task set as schedulable, a negative value implies otherwise. As can be seen in figs. 4(a),(b) and (c) all the 1000 generated task sets having 2,3, and 4 tasks are schedulable, thus validating the correctness of our schedulability conditions. VII. RELATED WORK Schedulability analysis of P-FRP have been presented in ( [8], [11]). In [11], a method to compute approximate values on WCRT has derived, however this method fails to converge on several task sets. A method to compute the actual response time under a given release scenario has been presented in [3]. None of these prior works derive any utilization based scheduling conditions for P-FRP.

Related work also deals with execution models similar, but not exactly same, as P-FRP. Primarily these are the lockfree execution and transactional memory (TM) [7]. Response time studies for the former are available in the works of Anderson et al [1]. Fahmy et al [6] do response time analysis of Transactional Memory implemented in software. Utilization based schedulability studies for both these execution models have also not been presented yet.

div.head: VIII. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
div.p: We have derived a sufficient schedulability condition for P-FRP task sets and validated its correctness using experimental task sets. This work has shown that a P-FRP n-task set is guaranteed to be schedulable when the total utilization factor of the task set is less than or equal to n 1 . In deriving this sufficient condition, we have considered a pessimistic scenario, which may not be applicable to practical task sets.

However such pessimism is important to provide the guarantee in the sufficient bound. The utilization bound derived by us is independent of the priority assignment scheme present in a P-FRP task set. This is important because as demonstrated by us in [4], the rate-monotonic priority assignment is not optimal in P-FRP, and an optimal priority assignment is so far unknown for this execution model.

In ongoing work, we will try to derive sufficient schedulability condition in the presence of blocking overheads, as well as determine ways in which the sufficient bound can be relaxed based on task set characteristics.
